records.name: Jordan
records.current_summary:
Jordan demands real caution from trans visitors — the safest of the Levantine Arab states by a clear margin, but on a deteriorating trajectory. Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in 1951, and courts have granted legal gender recognition in individual cases (the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling — though justified by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex). There is no statute criminalising gender expression itself.

The deterioration is documented: Cairo 52 reports a notable rise in targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, using Ottoman/British-era morality laws; Jordanian security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activities; the 2023 cybercrime law (“inciting immorality”) gives authorities a digital tool against LGBT expression; and gender-affirming surgery is criminalised for trans people (Article 8, Medical and Health Liability Law) while permitted for intersex people. In 2021 security forces arrested 14 people at a private party.

For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression per se, but morality-law discretion, shuttered community infrastructure, and family-society hostility make outing dangerous.
records.current_localsOnly: The criminalisation of gender-affirming surgery (Article 8) and the case-by-case LGR rulings are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: Surgery criminalisation and LGR case law are resident-facing; morality-law and cybercrime enforcement are the traveler-relevant mechanisms.

sources.claim: CAIRO 52 Jordan country profile: new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access; security forces coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave; intersex people can change legal gender markers but transgender people cannot, and gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

OutRight International Jordan profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations are NOT criminalised — Jordan abolished the colonial-era ban in 1951; no clear legal pathway for trans people to change gender markers (allowed 'in some cases'); gender-affirming surgery permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018.

HRW World Report 2024 Jordan chapter (11 Jan 2024): authorities limited civic space in 2023 and enacted a new cybercrime law undermining free speech and privacy online; peaceful dissidents and journalists arrested and harassed under vague, abusive laws, with intrusive digital surveillance — the environment shaping online expression for visitors and locals alike.

CAIRO 52 analysis of Case No. 2092/2014 (Jordan): Jordanian legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties up to 10 years' imprisonment (except intersex cases); the plaintiff (born 1977) sought name and gender change from male to female in official records after undergoing hormone therapy and surgery in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically.

HRW (6 Jun 2024): in Egypt, Jordan and Kuwait, same-sex relations are not explicitly criminalised in some, yet authorities 'legally' harass LGBT people via public-morality and debauchery laws — alternative legal avenues substitute for formal criminalisation, so decriminalisation on paper does not equal safety.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - despite state-sponsored repression and stigma, LGBT people are speaking out, building alliances and regional movements; includes an annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA (Jordan among them).

HRW (4 Dec 2023): Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality; officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation and social-media users posted their photos with messages inciting violence — two LGBT organisation directors cited official intimidation.

records.name: Venezuela
records.current_summary:
Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

Caracas has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.
records.current_localsOnly: The degraded healthcare including HRT access is resident-facing; the post-2024 persecution wave primarily affects resident activists and communities.
records.current_outOfScope: General humanitarian and repression context affects all travelers; the score reflects the trans-specific protection vacuum.

sources.claim: Washington Blade (10 Sep 2024): LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after the disputed July 2024 election; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 Sep 2024 -- persecution of LGBTQ people tied to the political crisis, dated.

EUAA asylum country-focus (reference period through 2025): dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in Venezuela used for international protection decisions -- the EU asylum agency's factual baseline on how LGBTIQ+ people are treated.
NOTE: The AFS/Vance Center LGBTQ guide on Venezuela (Oct 2024) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.

Blog record (31 Jan 2014): an equal-marriage bill was set to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week (per Aporrea) -- legislative push for same-sex marriage, historic milestone (no later enactment recorded).

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

records.name: Bolivia
records.current_summary:
Bolivia is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's legal pioneers on paper. The 2016 Gender Identity Law was ground-breaking: legal gender recognition on the basis of self-declared identity (administrative process, no surgery), and gender identity is an explicitly protected ground in anti-discrimination law. Bolivia's constitution also names gender identity.

Implementation lags the statute: the first national LGBTQ+ survey (2024) reveals significant exclusion in health, education, employment, and housing; social conservatism is strong outside La Paz/Santa Cruz; and bureaucrats often resist applying the Gender Identity Law. There is no documented pattern of police targeting of trans people as such, and no traveler-facing restriction — but also limited effective protection outside major cities.
records.current_localsOnly: The Gender Identity Law's administrative process, and its uneven implementation by bureaucrats, are resident-facing; the 2024 survey exclusion data describes residents' lives.
records.current_outOfScope: LGR mechanics and discrimination-law enforcement gaps are resident-facing.

sources.claim: Comparative Politics article (April 2024) 'Activists, Parties, and the Expansion of Trans Rights in Bolivia': Bolivia prohibits gender-identity discrimination and passed a ground-breaking gender identity law (2016, allowing name/marker change) despite low voter support; trans activists leveraged access to ruling-party legislators; contradictory heteronormative laws passed alongside because both organised religion and LGBT activists were party constituents.

NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (WordPress critical error); the underlying Agencia Presentes article (Dec 2024) covers Bolivia's first virtual survey revealing the great exclusion of LGBTI people.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Bolivia: general human-rights assessment (arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions, corruption) - the LGBT section documents the constitutional anti-discrimination guarantee and societal discrimination.

Newsweek (Jul 2017): after the US trans military ban, only 18 countries are believed to fully legalise LGBT military service — international baseline for whether trans visitors/soldiers face service exclusion; Bolivia not singled out in the text.

Legal-profile page: Constitution prohibits discrimination and guarantees bodily integrity (Art 15(II) violence, 45(V) maternity), Penal Code Title VIII governs abortion. Superseded by post-2016 law: 2016 gender-identity law (self-ID), Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion, Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition for same-sex couples.

eju.tv/La Razón (25 Aug 2014, Spanish): homosexuality is taboo in Bolivia's armed forces — gay soldiers report discrimination and sanctions, testimony given anonymously; the TLGB collective and human-rights activists demand openness.

freshness_all.fact: Post-2017 developments the archived sources miss: Jan-2018 Inter-American Court opinion; Dec-2020 civil-registry 'free union' recognition; 2016 gender-identity law remains a world-leading baseline. 2024 article still current.

records.name: Paraguay
records.current_summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors — South America's most conservative country. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ Paraguayans feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, Asunción has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.
records.current_localsOnly: The ten pending LGR lawsuits and the discrimination-law absence are resident-facing; the hometown-flight pattern describes residents.
records.current_outOfScope: Pending LGR lawsuits and discrimination-law absence are resident-facing.

sources.claim: AP (Sep 2025): 'For Paraguay's transgender women, survival often means leaving home' — discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of hometowns into migration and sex work.

Amnesty International Paraguay page (2025-26): trans people face obstacles to legal identity-document recognition - two trans migrants were denied identity documents; Asuncion's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March; plus 37 registered feminicides in 2025 and April's bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

ecoi / US State Dept reporting: judiciary had yet to issue final rulings on 10 lawsuits filed by trans people for legal name recognition - plaintiffs Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepulveda (suits since 2016) awaited a UN Human Rights Committee decision on their ICCPR Optional Protocol communications. Documented pace of recognition litigation.

PinkNews (20 Oct 2017): political climate report - ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes said he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man (later apologised to those offended); frames the report's account of a push to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'. Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric.

Tico Times (10 Jan 2018): on the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage - notes Bolivia, Paraguay and Peru recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, i.e. the ruling binds Paraguay (OAS party) though local law lagged; ~300 Costa Ricans celebrated at the court. Inter-American framework applying to Paraguay.

ABC Color (30 May 2017): adoption analysis - Law 1136/97 does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or singles from adopting (prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records), a legal gap allowing same-sex adoption as couples or as single men/women, amid a society that still closes doors. Adoption-law reality check.

Ultima Hora: post-IACtHR ruling analysis says people in Paraguay must overcome difficulties adapting the country's laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone - the domestic-law gap the inter-American opinion leaves for Paraguay to close.

records.name: Guatemala
records.current_summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (Law 5276, the 2022 “Life and Family Protection” law, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (Lambda, trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas (Antigua, Atitlán) are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.
records.current_localsOnly: The femicide-law exclusion of trans women and the pending LGR absence are resident-facing; the 147-case/29-murder toll falls on residents.
records.current_outOfScope: General gang violence affects all travelers; femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing but signals institutional stance.

sources.claim: Wikipedia article on transfemicide: documents killings of trans women; for Guatemala records that Central American governments have long excluded trans women from femicide protections — Guatemalan officials have justified this by stating that transgender women are not 'biological women' — the official exclusion underpinning the record's violence context.

Arcus Foundation report (May 2024): the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, but a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four countries.

HRW (Jan 2022): 'Guatemala: Anti-Trans Bill Threatens Rights' — documents legislative attacks on trans people, including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.

Washington Blade (Jan 2018): Latin American countries including Guatemala urged to abide by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruling (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) requiring marriage equality and gender recognition — compliance status uncertain.

records.name: Honduras
records.current_summary:
Honduras is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the hemisphere's defining transfemicide case: Vicky Hernández, a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the Inter-American Court of Human Rights — which in 2021 found the Honduran state itself responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which Honduras has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels Amnesty called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the Vicky Hernández ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the hemisphere outside Brazil/Mexico.
records.current_localsOnly: The IACHR-ordered LGR reform (partially implemented) and the name-change process are resident-facing; the epidemic-level violence and mass asylum-seeking describe residents' situation.
records.current_outOfScope: Gang violence affects everyone; the score reflects the trans-specific documented pattern and state-responsibility finding.

sources.claim: Wikipedia 'Transfemicide' (fetched 2026-09-29): general concept article with substantial Honduras content — HRW's El Salvador/Guatemala/Honduras finding that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks (Guatemalan officials calling them 'not biological women'), and Vicky Hernandez v Honduras at the Inter-American Court as the leading transfemicide case. Background framing for the record's violence claims.

LAWG Education Fund report 'Left in the Dark': Honduras and El Salvador among the world's highest rates of violence against women/LGBTI persons; LGBTI persons — trans women especially — face major obstacles to justice; impunity driven by under-reporting, lack of police/prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling (quote: institutions 'fail to effectively investigate and prosecute'). Explains why anti-trans violence goes unpunished.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Central America's LGBT people being terrorised at home and fleeing for their lives.

HRW report (May 2009) 'Not Worth a Penny': Human Rights Abuses against Transgender People in Honduras - police rape, assault and extortion of trans people, the shape of transgender lives in Honduras, and relevant domestic laws.

GlobalGayz Honduras archive: dated index of LGBT news 2004-2011 with embedded excerpts — Aug 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups; 2009-10 items ('Young LGBT Activist Murdered in Wave of Violence and Impunity', 'Extreme levels of violence against gay community', post-coup abuses); 2005 marriage/adoption-ban coverage. Source index corroborating the record's violence timeline rather than analysis.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras: significant human-rights issues include violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption, and lack of accountability for gender-based violence.

Washington Blade (25 Sep 2017): trans activist and Asociacion Cozumel Trans co-founder (PINU party) ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan at the 26 Nov 2017 election — potentially the first openly trans officeholder; context: Kendra Stefani Jordany's 2017 primary win, Claudia Spellman's 2012 LIBRE run, Victoria Gomez seeking asylum in Spain after threats/attacks in Tegucigalpa. Evidence of both trans visibility and the security costs behind it.

records.name: El Salvador
records.current_summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception with mass arbitrary detention (75,000+ imprisoned, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.
records.current_localsOnly: The administrative name-change-only process and the absent LGR law are resident-facing; the historical life-expectancy figure and the Díaz Córdova case describe residents.
records.current_outOfScope: The state of exception affects all travelers; its trans-specific application is a risk mechanism, not a documented pattern.

sources.claim: Foreign Policy (9 Mar 2020, Anna-Catherine Brigida): prosecution of the death of Camila Díaz Córdova, a transgender Salvadoran woman, as a hate crime — activists called it an advance toward El Salvador's first hate-crime homicide conviction while documenting continuing discrimination and abuse of LGBTQ citizens.

Dilemas journal article (Arévalo et al., Fundação Oswaldo Cruz, 2024): 'Denied deaths' builds a profile of crimes, victims and perpetrators of homicides against LGBTI+ people in El Salvador across 2000-2020 — the peer-reviewed longitudinal dataset on anti-LGBTI+ killings for the period.

HRW report 'Every Day I Live in Fear' (7 Oct 2020): El Salvador (with Guatemala and Honduras) fails to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims to the US; documents obstacles to obtaining protection.

HRW report (Jan 2021) 'I'm Lucky to Still Be Alive': violence and discrimination against LGBT people in El Salvador - full report with recommendations to the president, attorney general, congress and ministries.

HRW (31 Jul 2020): San Salvador judge found three police officers guilty of the January 2019 killing of transgender woman Camila Díaz Córdova and sentenced each to 20 years; the 28 July 2020 judgment is the first homicide conviction in El Salvador for killing a transgender person, hailed by HRW as pivotal for transgender Salvadorans' rights.

Washington Blade (9 Sep 2015): National Assembly approved legal-code reforms so killings motivated by sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, political affiliation or gender draw 30-60 years under Article 129 — the enhanced hate-crime penalty framework on the books since.

records.name: Dominican Republic
records.current_summary:
The Dominican Republic demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct between civilians is legal, but strikingly, Articles 210/260 still criminalise it for police and armed-forces members — challenged at the Constitutional Court in August 2024, revealing the institutional culture. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering SOGI (Brazil formally recommended one at the 2024 UPR), and documented violence against trans women is high, particularly affecting the most marginalised.

Tourist zones (Punta Cana, Puerto Plata) are heavily insulated resort enclaves with international norms; Santo Domingo has a visible community and annual Pride caravan. Outside those bubbles, machista culture, police harassment of trans women (especially sex workers), and anti-Haitian dynamics that compound for dark-skinned trans people are documented.
records.current_localsOnly: No LGR and no SOGI anti-discrimination law — resident-facing gaps; the police/military sodomy articles apply to residents in uniform, not civilians or visitors.
records.current_outOfScope: The police/military sodomy articles do not apply to civilians or visitors; resort vs. non-resort risk differs sharply.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (30 Aug 2024): documented the Constitutional Court challenge to sodomy-law remnants reaching only police and military officers (no equivalent for heterosexual acts), with HRW's amicus brief arguing equality/privacy violations. SUPERSEDED per resolved review: The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

UPR database (Sexual Rights Initiative): the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity — an accepted international-commitment record with no domestic implementation detail shown.

Time/Amnesty International (31 Mar 2019): TDOV conversation with two activists including Nairovi Castillo of the Dominican Republic, executive director of COTRAVETD (Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers, co-founded 2004) — first-hand account of trans struggles in the country.

Washington Blade (1 Apr 2017): 300+ activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo with Dominican government officials speaking — a marker of official-level engagement in 2017.

Washington Blade (27 Apr 2016): documents the backlash against openly gay US Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo — framed as attacks on LGBT Dominicans, showing organised domestic opposition climate.

Washington Blade (3 Apr 2017): the openly gay US ambassador's departure left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence (spoke at Santo Domingo Pride, 3 Jul 2016) — trailing marker of the polarised climate his tenure exposed.

freshness_all.fact: The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

evidence.title: LGBTQ rights in the Dominican Republic
